lines.text: Why does weight move? Look at the robot from the side.
Its balance point, the center of mass, sits at height h. We'll use twenty centimeters as an example.
The wheels sit a distance x in front and behind. Our modules are ten inches out: zero point two five four meters.
Speeding up, the floor pushes the tires forward with m times a, h below the balance point.
A push below the balance point makes a turning effect, a moment: force times lever arm, here m times a times h.
It tries to tip the robot back, nose up. The robot doesn't tip, so something balances it.
The wheel loads do. Each back wheel gains an amount, delta N. Each front wheel loses the same.
Four wheels, each delta N, each x from the middle: a balancing moment of four times delta N times x.
Set the moments equal: delta N equals m a h, over four x.
So each wheel carries m g over four, plus delta N at the back, minus delta N at the front.
At six meters per second squared, delta N is seventy-one newtons. Front wheels carry seventy-six, back wheels two hundred eighteen.
At ten, the front wheels carry only twenty-nine newtons. Their budget is almost gone.
At zero front load, the robot tips: g x over h, twelve point five meters per second squared.
